-1 may be neutralized. You could even make a case for -2 being neutralized. -3 is clearly not neutralized, as when the Foundation tested it, it did something.

The anomaly isn't the time traveller, the anomaly is her origin, and we haven't solved it yet.

item.title: Backstory
item.content:encoded:
I figured it out.

I know where she came from.

I know why her machine was disassembled. I know why the parts are being kept in separate locations, and the number of locations is blackboxed, and it's forbidden to bring any of the parts within 100 km of each other, and you need written permission from two separate O5s in order to examine even one of the parts, and the mechanical schematics and circuit diagrams she was making are restricted-access.

The phrase "time machine" is usually taken to mean that it goes back and/or forth in time, but it actually moves sideways. She's from another timeline.

But her timeline-crossing machine requires all the energy in the universe. She can never go back to her universe, because activating the machine and hopping to another universe, obliterates the universe you just left. (Randall Garrett did a short story with this premise, and Shaenon Garrity used a variant in Narbonic.)

This is why the data pertaining to how the machine works, and what it can do, and what fields of knowledge you need to study in order to build one just like it… was not just redacted, but expunged.

SCP-317 was trying to teach the Foundation to help her repair/rebuild her machine so she could leave. Did she know that what she was doing would have led to the Foundation's entire universe being obliterated? If she did, would she have cared?

How many universes did she obliterate before her machine caught fire, stranding her?

How close was the Foundation to being reduced to fuel?

item.content:encoded:
…WELL THEN.

I guess instead of that wall of text I could have just pointed out that 'primates' covers monkeys, too. And, I guess, that some dinos still matched lower-level primates. Dammit. Oh well, it was fun to write.

I also realized I omitted numbers in my original post. Unfortunately EQ numbers follow several different scales, so hard numbers can be difficult to find on The Internets, so here's a limited array of common dinosaurs vs common animals.

The smartest dinos were (so far as we know) ornithomimids at 0.8 and troodontids 0.7, hitting the lower-level primate level (lemurs/langurs). We can extrapolate that smaller theropods were around this level, especially the later ones; I can't find an EQ for a velociraptor in the up-to-date system, but it's supposedly about the same as a troodontid, which is in fact terrifyingly intelligent… The big herd animals of the Cretaceous, hadrosaurs and iguanodontids, fared pretty well at approx 0.5. By comparison, the elephant is 0.6 - and it's pretty common knowledge how smart elephants are. Hippos are a bit under 0.3 (so were things like Triceratops), warthogs 0.4. There were some dinosaurs that brushed the lower end of the scale - mostly sauropods with their tiny little heads. Most animals fall into the 0 to 1 range. Cats are 1, dogs are about 1.1, probably due to selection pressures to breed more trainable dogs. Dolphins get higher, with the bottlenose getting a 3.6. Non-human primates span the range from a little under 1 and 4, with humans taking the top at a whopping 5.

I can't find chickens either, unfortunately :P

(…oh gawd, just occurred to me, elephants can learn to open doors, velociraptors were smarter than elephants by this measurement… noooooooooo)

(of course elephants also have prehensile trunks and raptors don't so I am overstating things a little there ;d)

Also, goddammit, all this unnecessary Googling uncovered a recent research paper in which it posits that pachycephalosaurids may have had bigger brains then we thought; there's a debate on how much of their heads were filled with connective tissue and how much was actual brain. Scientists used to assume that pachys used their dome heads like rams do, but now it's understood that they were probably more for display and flank-butting (much less hardcore than head-butting). So they may actually have had average brains, not especially tiny ones. Goddammit. I fail as scientific advisor. SCIENCE MARCHES ON~

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Whoa there. Even the smartest dinosaur was probably still only as smart as a chicken. Maybe slightly dumber, even.

WARNING: DINOSAUR NERD TIME

I thought that troodontids being relatively smart was common knowledge after Dale Russell's silly "Dinosauroid" ended up in a bunch of pop dinosaur books.

We don't actually know how smart dinosaurs were for sure. However, modern estimates of ridiculously low dinosaur intellect were based on using brain volume estimates from modern-day reptiles, when in reality dinosaurs were much more like modern-day birds.

Why does this make a difference, you ask? See, reptiles generally have brains that take up about fifty percent of their braincases. Birds and mammals have brains that take up all their braincases. Until recently, birds were thought of as 'what dinosaurs evolved into'; rather, birds are the modern surviving branch of dinosaur, and share traits that most dinosaurs had. Like reasonably sized brains. But no one believed this until paleontologists finally started actually examining the braincase interior more closely in recent findings (most relevantly, Psittacosaurus, if I recall correctly).

This is basically the same issue as people having their minds explode when they're told that most small dinosaurs had pseudo-fur (ornithopods) or feathers, including small wings (theropods). It's just more traditional to assume that dinos were stupid. (Though, the hyper-intelligent Velociraptors of Jurassic Park were, uh, a bit much.)

In conclusion, dinosaurs were about twice as smart as we thought they were before less than a decade ago. Comparable to modern-day mammals and birds, with some variation.

…because I can't stop editing: I should also point out that dinosaur/bird brains were/are structured completely differently from mammal brains. For instance, they didn't/don't even have cerebral cortexes. And that's not even getting into variation within categories. There's a reason why we can't pin down just how smart whales are - there's evidence that they're very intelligent, but we can't even comprehend how certain parts of their brain work. And then you have more "primitive" invertebrates like octopi demonstrating exceptionally high intelligence. And then there's the issue of how powerful your senses are… Etc, etc, etc.

Revenge of the edit: A good comparison is that the smartest known dinosaurs were probably around as smart as the lower level monkeys, but not apes. Also keep in mind that the smartest known dinosaurs were also pretty small, so there are fewer traces of them in the fossil record, just like there are few traces of primates in the fossil record; this means there were probably a whole lot more of them scurrying through the undergrowth than we've actually found. Just… not pachycephalosaurids.

item.content:encoded:
This appeals to me. It's mysterious, tragic in a certain light, and lends itself equally well to any number of mutually exclusive explanations. Parallel history? Maybe. Altered, no-longer-existent timeline? Could be. Alien with semi-convergent evolution who's lying to keep us from suspecting her peoples' existence? No evidence against it. The final comment about the lack of fossil records is a great way of hanging a lantern on the entire issue.

The infection death is a wonderful conclusion, fittingly scientific and providing a tidy reason for why we don't know more. Although I wonder why she didn't catch something sooner? Maybe she had a stock of rations (a reasonable preparation for an expedition into the unknown) and caught the bug when they ran out and she was forced to rely on modern food?

It feels empty though. If interviews were possible, the purpose of the "tools" should have been easily determined. A basic history of her civilization should have been easy to convey, including geologic markers as to the time period she lived in (how many continents, what shape were they arranged in). I feel like we should know a LOT more with that much time to grill someone from a highly advanced civilization.

I still like the concept though. I'd imagine the simplest explanation (amusingly complex as it is) is that her civilization created a time machine that could travel back in time, but didn't realize that a massive release of destructive energy occurred after the machine leaves for another time. That would:
1. Destroy her unfortunate civilization as she went back in time to explore the Cretaceous period
2. Create a new timeline for us on her arrival
3. Cause the extinction event of our timeline when she left, thus depositing her into our timeline when she tried to return to her starting point

In that scenario, the poor girl would have no fucking idea why there are a bunch of big mammals running around. And if someone pointed out the Cretaceous extinction, she'd be totally justified in:
"Oh my god… I'm back. I'm home. All the time it was… I finally really did it… I maniac! I blew it up! Damn me… God damn me all to hell!"
